# Probability, and how a machine learns it {#sec-ch02}

::: {.epigraph by="Joseph Butler, The Analogy of Religion, 1736"}
But to us, probability is the very guide of life.
:::

"Probability? Coins and dice. I don't need it to build AI." That thought is the most expensive mistake in this field. This chapter makes sure you can read a chance without being fooled, and shows how a machine learns one.

::: {.goals}
- Say what "70%" means in a way you could check.
- Spot the base-rate trap, and update a probability by multiplying odds.
- Explain how a machine learns a probability, and how it fools you.
:::

## What "70%" means

Your weather app says 70% chance of rain. It stays dry. Was it wrong? One day can't tell you. The forecaster's *record* can: across every day they said "70%", did it rain on about 70 of every 100?

::: {.keyidea}
A **probability** is a claim about how often something happens among cases like this one.
:::

This definition matters because you can *check* it. A model that calls an alert "70% likely" makes the weather app's promise, and can be checked the same way.

## The trap that fools doctors

Try this before reading on. A detector catches 99% of real attacks and raises a false alarm on 5% of normal activity. Real attacks are rare: one event in a thousand. The detector fires. What's the chance it's a real attack?

Most people say about 95%. The answer is about **2%**. In a famous 1978 study, doctors at Harvard Medical School got the same puzzle about a medical test, and the most common answer was 95% [@casscells1978].

![The same puzzle, counted out. Of 100,000 events, 100 are attacks and the detector catches 99 of them. But 5% of the 99,900 normal events also set it off: 4,995 false alarms. When the alarm sounds, you're holding one of 5,094 alerts, and only 99 of them are real.](/figures/ch02/base-rate-tree.pdf){#fig-base-rate-tree}

The way out is to count (@fig-base-rate-tree). The 5% false-alarm rate is 5% of a *huge* number; the 99% hit rate is 99% of a *tiny* one. The chance before any evidence, here 1 in 1,000, is the **base rate**, and ignoring it is the most common probability mistake there is. It's why a "95% accurate" fraud model can drown a bank in false alarms. Whenever a probability surprises you, turn it into counts [@gigerenzer1995].

::: {.keyidea}
Rare things stay rare even after the alarm goes off.
:::

A related trap: "how often do attacks look like this?" is not "how often is something that looks like this an attack?" Only {{< num ch02 ioc_attack_share pct >}} of attacks come with a bad threat score, but that doesn't make a bad-score alert {{< num ch02 ioc_attack_share pct >}} likely to be one; it's {{< num ch02 p1 pct >}}. In court, mixing the two up is the *prosecutor's fallacy*, and it has jailed innocent people.

## Bayes' rule in one line

How *should* a clue change your mind? Use **odds**: 20% is odds of 20 to 80, or 0.25. Each clue has a strength, its **likelihood ratio**: how much more common it is among attacks than among harmless alerts. A bad threat score is about {{< num ch02 lr_ioc f1 >}} times more common among attacks.

::: {.keyidea}
New odds = old odds × likelihood ratio.
:::

An ordinary alert starts at {{< num ch02 base pct >}}. A bad threat score takes it to {{< num ch02 p1 pct >}}; "outside business hours" to {{< num ch02 p2 pct >}}; "sign-in from a new country" to {{< num ch02 p3 pct >}}. One warning: this assumes each clue says something *new*. Real clues overlap, so in practice we let a model learn how much each is worth.

![Starting from the base rate and multiplying the odds by each clue's likelihood ratio. Three ordinary clues take an alert from "probably nothing" to "probably an attack".](/figures/ch02/odds-update.pdf){#fig-odds-update}

## Why accuracy lies

Score the rule *flag any alert with a threat score of 0.5 or more*. **Precision**, how often a flag is real, is {{< num ch02 precision pct >}}. **Recall**, how many attacks it catches, is {{< num ch02 recall pct >}}. **Accuracy**, the share of all alerts judged correctly, is {{< num ch02 accuracy pct >}}. Sounds good, until you see that flagging *nothing at all* scores {{< num ch02 always_benign_acc pct >}}. When one outcome is rare, accuracy mostly measures how common the other one is.

![Every one of the 20,000 alerts, sorted by what the rule said and what really happened. Precision and recall each ignore one of the two columns, which makes them fair judges of rare events.](/figures/ch02/confusion.pdf){#fig-confusion}

## How a machine learns a probability

Bayes multiplies odds; adding is easier. Take the logarithm of the odds and multiplication becomes addition. That gives a simple machine: start from a base number, add a **weight** for each clue, and turn the total into a probability with an S-shaped curve. That's **logistic regression**, behind credit and medical risk scores for decades. It learns all the weights *together*, so overlapping clues aren't counted twice.

![The S-curve (the logistic, or sigmoid, function) turns total evidence into a probability. Every step to the right multiplies the odds by the same amount, which is why the curve flattens out: once you're very sure, more evidence changes the probability only a little.](/figures/ch03/sigmoid.pdf){#fig-sigmoid}

To set the weights, we need to score a probability. Say 90% and be right: lose almost nothing. Say 1% and be wrong: lose a lot, for being confidently wrong. That score is **log loss**, a measure of surprise.

![Log loss for a single alert. If it really was an attack (red, solid curve), the penalty is small when the model gave "attack" a high probability. It grows very fast as that probability gets close to zero. Harmless alerts (blue, dashed curve) work the same way from the other side.](/figures/ch03/logloss.pdf){#fig-logloss}

Log loss has a property the whole book leans on. It's a **proper scoring rule**: the only way to score best on average is to report what you actually believe (@fig-logloss). Exaggerate, and over many cases you lose. So models trained on log loss tend to come out honest, or *calibrated*.

Training is a walk downhill. Picture log loss as hilly ground, where each combination of weights is a place. Stand in thick fog, feel which way the ground slopes, step downhill, repeat. That's **gradient descent**. Run on our alerts and tested on alerts held back from training, it comes within {{< num ch03 gap_pct pct >}} of the best score any model could reach.

::: {.keyidea}
All of machine learning is one loop: predict, measure the surprise, step downhill.
:::

Training an LLM is the same loop with a vastly bigger model.

## Two ways a model fools you

**Overfitting** is memorising instead of learning. A decision tree allowed twenty levels of yes-or-no questions nearly memorises its training alerts (loss {{< num ch03 tree_deep_train f3 >}}) and does badly on new ones ({{< num ch03 tree_deep_test f2 >}}). You only see it by testing on data the model never trained on.

![A decision tree allowed only a few questions learns general patterns. Allowed dozens, it memorises individual training alerts: its loss on them approaches zero while its loss on new alerts climbs.](/figures/ch03/overfit.pdf){#fig-overfit}

**Leakage** is a clue that secretly contains the answer. Train with analysts' notes and results look amazing, because "confirmed phishing" is written *after* someone decided. Ask of every clue: *would I have this value at the moment of the decision?*

::: {.exercises}
1. A spam filter catches 98% of spam and wrongly flags 1% of real email. If only 1% of incoming email is spam, what fraction of flagged emails are real? Use counts.
:::
